questions.stem: Which three places mark the corners of the Polynesian Triangle?
options: Fiji, Aotearoa New Zealand and Tahiti
Papua New Guinea, Hawai‘i and Tonga
Hawai‘i, Aotearoa New Zealand and Rapa Nui
Hawai‘i, Australia and Rapa Nui (Easter Island)
questions.explanation: Polynesia is a huge triangle of ocean with Hawai‘i to the north, Aotearoa New Zealand to the south-west and Rapa Nui (Easter Island) to the east, and islands such as Tahiti, Samoa and Tonga inside it. Australia lies well outside it, and its First Nations peoples arrived tens of thousands of years earlier by a different route. Fiji and Papua New Guinea are usually grouped with Melanesia.

questions.stem: Why is Lapita pottery important evidence for the settlement of the Pacific?
options: It proves that the first settlers of Polynesia sailed west from the coast of South America
It shows Polynesians learnt pottery from the crew of Captain Cook in the 1700s
It was made in Aotearoa New Zealand and traded north-west as far as China
Its spread traces the ancestors of Polynesians from near New Guinea to Tonga and Samoa
questions.explanation: Distinctive stamped Lapita pottery appears in the Bismarck Archipelago near New Guinea about 3300 years ago and then, within a few centuries, in Vanuatu, Fiji, Tonga and Samoa, tracking the ancestors of Polynesians as they moved east. It points to origins in the west, not South America. Aotearoa was settled much later, long after Lapita pottery had stopped being made.

questions.stem: What kind of vessel did Polynesian voyagers use to settle distant islands?
options: Bark canoes paddled along the coast
Rafts made from logs of balsa wood
Wooden sailing ships with iron nails
Large double-hulled sailing canoes
questions.explanation: Polynesians built large double-hulled canoes (waka hourua in Māori, va‘a in Samoan and Tahitian) with sails, able to carry people, plants and animals across thousands of kilometres of open ocean. Balsa rafts are linked to Thor Heyerdahl's Kon-Tiki experiment, not to Polynesian voyaging. Polynesians did not use metal, so their canoes were lashed together with fibre cord.

questions.stem: How did Polynesian navigators find their way across the open ocean without instruments?
options: By using magnetic compasses obtained through trade with merchants from China
By following paper maps that were passed down and copied from one generation to the next
By staying within sight of land and hopping only between neighbouring islands
By reading the stars, ocean swells, the flight of birds and clouds over islands
questions.explanation: Wayfinders memorised where stars rose and set, felt the direction of ocean swells through the hull, watched land-based birds and noticed clouds that build up over islands. This knowledge was passed down orally and through training, not on paper maps. Many voyages crossed long stretches far out of sight of land.

questions.stem: In 1947 Thor Heyerdahl sailed the raft Kon-Tiki from Peru to Polynesia to support which theory?
options: That Polynesia was first settled from Asia by deliberate voyaging
That Polynesians had sailed on to reach and settle Australia
That Polynesians had reached Antarctica long before Europeans
That Polynesia was first settled from South America
questions.explanation: Heyerdahl believed people had drifted west from South America to settle Polynesia, and his voyage showed a raft could cross that distance. But language, Lapita pottery, DNA and archaeology all point to Polynesian ancestors coming from the west, from Island South-East Asia. Settlement from the west by skilled, deliberate voyaging is the view most researchers hold today.

questions.stem: Which evidence most strongly links the ancestors of Polynesians to Island South-East Asia rather than to South America?
options: The oldest settlements in all of Polynesia have been found on Rapa Nui
All the crops Polynesians grew had come from South America
Polynesian languages, Lapita pottery and DNA all point west towards Asia
Polynesian languages are closely related to Quechua, spoken in Peru and Bolivia
questions.explanation: Polynesian languages belong to the Austronesian family, which spread from Taiwan through Island South-East Asia, and Lapita pottery and DNA studies show the same east-moving trail. The oldest Polynesian sites are in the west, in Tonga and Samoa, while Rapa Nui was one of the last islands settled. Most Polynesian crops, such as taro, yams and breadfruit, came from the west; the sweet potato is the famous exception.

questions.stem: Why is the sweet potato important in debates about Polynesian voyaging?
options: It grew wild on every Pacific island, so voyagers never needed to carry crops with them
It is a South American plant that Polynesians grew before Europeans came, suggesting contact
It is an Asian plant whose spread across the Pacific exactly follows the trail of Lapita pottery
It was brought to the Pacific by Captain Cook, which proves Europeans introduced farming
questions.explanation: The sweet potato was first domesticated in the Americas, yet it was being grown in Polynesia centuries before Europeans arrived, so many researchers think Polynesian voyagers reached South America and brought it back. Polynesians already farmed taro, yams and breadfruit that they had carried from the west. Cook found sweet potatoes already being grown by Māori in Aotearoa.

questions.stem: Why was the 1976 voyage of the canoe Hokule‘a from Hawai‘i to Tahiti significant?
options: It proved that Polynesia had been settled by rafts drifting across from South America
It was the first time anyone had ever sailed between Hawai‘i and Tahiti
It showed that canoes could only drift with currents and could not sail into the wind
It showed long voyages were possible using only traditional navigation
questions.explanation: Hokule‘a, a replica double-hulled canoe, sailed more than 4000 kilometres to Tahiti guided by the master navigator Mau Piailug using stars, swells and birds, with no compass or charts. This supported the view that Polynesian settlement was deliberate rather than accidental drift. Hawaiian traditions already recorded voyages between Hawai‘i and Tahiti centuries earlier.

questions.stem: Most evidence suggests the ancestors of Māori first settled Aotearoa New Zealand around:
options: 40 000 years ago
1000 BCE
questions.explanation: Radiocarbon dates, volcanic ash layers and other evidence point to settlement in the late 1200s, making Aotearoa one of the last large land masses on Earth to be settled by people. 1642 is when the Dutch explorer Abel Tasman arrived. Tens of thousands of years ago is the timescale for First Nations Australians in Sahul, not for Aotearoa.

questions.stem: What happened to the moa after people settled Aotearoa New Zealand?
options: They survived in large flocks until European settlers began hunting them in the 1800s
Hunting and habitat loss drove these giant birds to extinction within a few centuries
They were domesticated and farmed in large numbers for their meat, eggs and feathers
They were carried on voyaging canoes to Hawai‘i, where they were kept as sacred birds
questions.explanation: The moa, some species standing over 3 metres tall with their necks raised, had no fear of humans because Aotearoa had no land mammals that hunted them. Hunting, egg collecting and the burning of forests drove all species extinct within a few centuries of settlement, well before Europeans arrived. Their loss led to changes in Māori food sources and ways of life.

questions.stem: What was a rahui in Māori and other Polynesian societies?
options: A temporary ban on taking a resource so that it could recover
A gift exchanged between two iwi to seal a peace agreement
A large carved canoe used for war and ceremonies
The title given to the highest-ranking chief of a whole iwi
questions.explanation: A rahui places a restriction, backed by tapu, on taking fish, shellfish, birds or plants from an area for a time, letting them recover; it can also follow a death or disaster. It shows Polynesian systems for managing resources sustainably. Rahui are still declared in Aotearoa today, for example to protect fisheries.

questions.stem: Which list orders traditional Māori social groups from largest to smallest?
options: iwi, whānau, hapū
iwi, hapū, whānau
whānau, hapū, iwi
hapū, iwi, whānau
questions.explanation: The iwi is the tribe, made up of several hapū (sub-tribes or clans), each of which is made up of whānau (extended families). All three are linked by whakapapa, shared descent from common ancestors. These groups remain central to Māori identity and organisation today.

questions.stem: In traditional Māori society, what was a tohunga?
options: A chief who led a hapū or iwi and spoke for its people in council meetings
A carved meeting house at the centre of a community
A temporary ban placed on an area to protect its resources
An expert with specialist knowledge, such as a priest, navigator or carver
questions.explanation: A tohunga was a skilled expert, such as a priest, healer, navigator, carver or builder, whose knowledge was often sacred. A leading chief was a rangatira (or ariki for the highest rank). A carved meeting house is a wharenui, and a temporary ban is a rahui.

questions.stem: Polynesian chiefs (ariki) were believed to hold great mana. What is mana?
options: Cloth made by beating the inner bark of trees until it is soft and thin
The double-hulled canoe in which ancestors first arrived
Spiritual power, authority and prestige, often inherited from ancestors
A sacred restriction placed on a person, object or place
questions.explanation: Mana is spiritual power, authority and prestige; chiefs inherited mana through their descent from gods and ancestors, and could gain or lose it through their actions. A sacred restriction is tapu, which protected the mana of chiefs and sacred places. Cloth made from beaten bark is tapa.

questions.stem: What is tapa?
options: A chant that records a family line back to the first ancestors
Cloth made by beating the inner bark of trees such as paper mulberry
A sacred restriction placed by a chief on a person, place or object
A stone statue carved to honour an important ancestor on the island of Rapa Nui
questions.explanation: Tapa (also called ngatu in Tonga and siapo in Samoa) is made by soaking and beating strips of inner bark, then decorating them with patterns, and is still made and gifted at important occasions. The sacred restriction is tapu, a similar-sounding word with a very different meaning. The statues of Rapa Nui are moai.

questions.stem: What did the moai of Rapa Nui represent?
options: Gods of the sea, set along the cliffs facing outward to guard against invaders
Dutch and Spanish sailors who visited the island in the 1700s
Warriors from Tahiti who died fighting the people of Rapa Nui
Important ancestors, set on platforms that mostly faced inland over villages
questions.explanation: The moai were carved mainly from volcanic tuff at the Rano Raraku quarry to honour important ancestors, and most stood on stone platforms (ahu) facing inland, watching over the communities they protected. The idea that they gaze out to sea is a common misconception. They were made centuries before any Europeans reached the island in 1722.

questions.stem: Rapa Nui oral traditions say the moai 'walked' to their platforms. How do recent experiments relate to this tradition?
options: They showed the statues were far too heavy to move, so each one was carved where it stands today
They proved the moai were floated around the coast on rafts, so the tradition must be wrong
They showed only European machines could have moved the statues from the quarry
Teams with ropes rocked an upright replica forward, so the tradition may describe a real method
questions.explanation: In 2012 researchers showed that a small team using ropes could 'walk' an upright replica moai by rocking it from side to side, which fits the oral tradition and the way statues abandoned along old roads lie. Most moai were carved at the Rano Raraku quarry and moved kilometres from it. The experiments show how oral traditions and archaeology can support each other.

questions.stem: Some writers have argued that the people of Rapa Nui destroyed their own society by cutting down all the island's trees. Why have many researchers challenged this view?
options: The population of Rapa Nui kept growing steadily until well into the twentieth century
The moai were found to have been carved from imported wood, so no local trees were ever needed
Rats that ate palm seeds, and diseases and slave raids after European contact, played major roles
The island never had any trees at all until Europeans planted forests in the 1800s
questions.explanation: The island's palm forests did disappear, but Polynesian rats introduced by the settlers ate the palm seeds, and the society adapted with new farming methods such as rock gardens. The greatest population collapse came after European contact, from introduced diseases and the Peruvian slave raids of the 1860s. The debate shows how the same evidence can support very different explanations.

questions.stem: Tupaia, a navigator and priest from Ra‘iatea who joined Captain Cook's Endeavour in 1769, is remembered for:
options: Drawing a chart of dozens of Pacific islands from his own knowledge
Leading the first Polynesian voyage that discovered and settled Hawai‘i
Becoming the first person to reach and settle Rapa Nui
Translating the whole Bible into the Māori and Tahitian languages
questions.explanation: Tupaia drew a chart showing dozens of islands across a vast area of the Pacific, recording Polynesian geographical knowledge for Cook's expedition, and acted as an interpreter when the Endeavour reached Aotearoa. Hawai‘i and Rapa Nui had been settled centuries before his time. His role shows how much European voyagers depended on Polynesian expertise.

questions.stem: Paul Gauguin's paintings of Tahiti in the 1890s show an exotic island paradise. What should a historian keep in mind when using them as a source?
options: They show a European artist's ideas about Polynesia more than real Tahitian lives
They are exact records of daily life, painted to be as accurate as any photographs
They were painted by Tahitian artists for local people to hang in their homes
They show Tahiti as it was before any European had visited the islands
questions.explanation: Gauguin, a French painter, presented Tahiti as an untouched paradise even though it had been under French control, with missionaries and traders, for decades. His paintings reveal European fantasies about the Pacific, which is valuable evidence of attitudes but not a reliable record of Tahitian life. Historians compare such representations with Polynesian sources and other evidence.
